title: Redwood Private (AWS VPC) networking deep dive + Terraform modules (alpha)
summary: BrightShield walked through their AWS network constraints (shared services VPC, transit gateway, strict egress controls, preference for private endpoints only). Redwood covered the default Private alpha AWS topology (public/private/isolated tiers), NAT strategies (single vs per-AZ vs centralized egress), and the required/optional VPC endpoints needed for the Private installer to pull images and emit logs (ECR api/dkr, S3 gateway, CloudWatch Logs, STS; SSM optional). Redwood explained how the alpha Terraform modules standardize these defaults and reduce deployment time/variance, plus what inputs allow existing VPC adoption. Customer asked for clarity on DNS/private hosted zones, PrivateLink vs interface endpoints, flow logs routing/retention, and how to validate preflight checks before running the installer.
topics: AWS VPC topology for Redwood Private (subnet tiers, routing, NAT options)
Required/optional VPC endpoints for installer and day-2 ops
Private DNS / Route53 considerations (private hosted zones, resolver, split-horizon)
Flow logs + centralized logging patterns (CloudWatch vs S3)
Existing VPC adoption mode and guardrails
Preflight validation checks and common failure modes
action_items: Colin O'Donnell: Send Terraform alpha quickstart + example tfvars for private-only endpoints/no public egress (by 2025-02-06).
Victor Alvarez: Share endpoint requirements list (ECR api/dkr, S3 gateway, CloudWatch Logs, STS; optional SSM) and note which are hard requirements for installer vs observability (by 2025-02-06).
Markus Klein: Schedule follow-up with BrightShield to review their existing VPC / TGW diagram and confirm NAT/egress approach (target next week).
Anita Desai: Provide current CIDR plan + subnets per AZ + whether they can create Route53 private hosted zones in the workload account (no date).
next_steps: Redwood to send quickstart and locked-down VPC example configuration.
BrightShield to confirm whether they want zero-internet egress and rely solely on VPC endpoints.
Set up a 60-min architecture review with BrightShield network team using their TGW/shared services constraints.
Optional: run Redwood installer networking preflight checks against their dev account once endpoints/DNS are in place.
transcript:
Meeting: Redwood x BrightShield — Private (AWS VPC) networking deep dive + Terraform modules (alpha)
Recorded: 2025-02-05 17:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees:
- Colin O'Donnell (Redwood)
- Markus Klein (Redwood)
- Victor Alvarez (Redwood)
- Anita Desai (BrightShield)
- Jordan Kim (BrightShield)
- Priya Nair (BrightShield)

Auto-Generated Summary (Fireflies)
- Discussed target VPC topology, endpoint requirements, DNS, and how reference Terraform modules reduce time to deploy.

Auto-Generated Action Items (Fireflies)
- Colin to send quickstart docs + sample tfvars.
- Victor to send endpoint matrix.
- BrightShield to share current VPC/TGW constraints.

---

[00:00] Colin O'Donnell: Alright, we’re recording. Thanks everyone. This is the networking deep dive for Redwood Private in AWS VPC and specifically the alpha Terraform modules we’ve been working on. Goal today is make sure we’re aligned on what you need in your environment, what’s required for the installer, and what’s optional.

[00:19] Anita Desai: Sounds good.

[00:20] Jordan Kim: Yep.

[00:21] Priya Nair: Good.

[00:23] Markus Klein: Cool. Maybe quick intros? I’m Markus, solutions at Redwood.

[00:27] Victor Alvarez: Victor, infra/networking at Redwood.

[00:29] Colin O'Donnell: And I’m Colin, I run pilot implementations on the solutions side.

[00:34] Anita Desai: I’m Anita, platform engineering lead. Jordan is our network architect and Priya is security.

[00:40] Colin O'Donnell: Great. Anita, do you want to start with the constraints? Like, what “good” looks like for your VPC.

[00:46] Anita Desai: Sure. So we run a multi-account setup. There’s a shared services VPC and then workload VPCs. Everything is behind a transit gateway. We prefer no public internet egress from workloads. If we absolutely need egress it has to go through a centralized proxy in shared services. Also DNS is… a little messy. We use Route53 private hosted zones but they’re controlled by a central account.

[01:12] Jordan Kim: And we’re pretty strict on endpoints. We like interface endpoints for APIs. For S3 we use gateway endpoints typically. No IGWs in workload VPCs, ideally.

[01:24] Priya Nair: Plus audit logging requirements. VPC flow logs on, retention set, and we need to know exactly what logs Redwood emits and where.

[01:34] Colin O'Donnell: Got it. That aligns with a lot of what we see. Victor can you outline the default alpha topology and then we’ll map it to “no internet” mode.

[01:43] Victor Alvarez: Yep. So our default baseline module creates a VPC with three subnet tiers per AZ: public, private, and isolated.
- Public is typically for NAT gateway, optional.
- Private is for data plane components that need outbound to AWS services, either via NAT or endpoints.
- Isolated is for things that should not route to NAT/IGW at all.

[02:09] Victor Alvarez: In the alpha we support two NAT modes: single NAT for cost, or per-AZ NAT for resilience. And then we also have a pattern we call “centralized egress” where you can disable NAT creation and route 0.0.0.0/0 to your TGW / egress VPC, but with guardrails because people can shoot themselves in the foot.

[02:29] Jordan Kim: Okay. For us, likely no NAT in the workload VPC, and route out through TGW to a proxy. But… we also prefer VPC endpoints if possible. So maybe we don’t need 0/0 at all.

[02:42] Markus Klein: That’s usually the cleanest: private-only endpoints and no default route to the internet. The main question becomes: do you have every endpoint we need, and does DNS resolve to them.

[02:53] Priya Nair: Which endpoints are “need” versus “nice to have”?

[02:57] Victor Alvarez: For the installer and core operation, the hard requirements are basically:
- ECR API (interface endpoint)
- ECR DKR (interface endpoint)
- S3 gateway endpoint (for image layers and sometimes artifacts)
- CloudWatch Logs (interface endpoint) if you want the simplest logging path; otherwise we can do log forwarding to your sink but CloudWatch is common
- STS (interface endpoint) is often required in locked-down environments because AWS SDK calls will fail if they can’t reach STS; some folks miss this.

[03:32] Victor Alvarez: Optional but common:
- SSM / EC2 Messages / SSM Messages if you’re doing any SSM-based management; we don’t require it for Redwood runtime itself but customers like it.

[03:47] Jordan Kim: For STS, we often rely on the public STS endpoint via centralized proxy. But if you’re saying the SDK calls will break, we can add the STS interface endpoint in the workload VPC.

[03:58] Colin O'Donnell: Yeah, we’ve seen exactly that: everything looks fine, then installer fails when trying to auth/pull or when components assume STS is reachable. In our preflight checks we explicitly test STS resolution/reachability.

[04:13] Priya Nair: Preflight checks… are those part of the installer or the Terraform?

[04:17] Colin O'Donnell: Installer. Terraform gives you the “known good” network pieces. Installer does checks like: can resolve ECR domains, can reach endpoints, can hit S3 via gateway, that kind of thing. If it fails, it tells you which endpoint is missing.

[04:34] Markus Klein: And part of why we did these reference modules is: too many one-off VPC builds, and the support burden goes way up. So we standardize the endpoints, DNS toggles, flow logs, tagging, outputs the installer needs.

[04:49] Anita Desai: What are the outputs? Like what does the installer consume.

[04:53] Victor Alvarez: Typically: VPC ID, subnet IDs by tier, security group IDs for the Redwood components, and the endpoint IDs and whether private DNS is enabled per endpoint. Also route table IDs sometimes for debugging.

[05:10] Jordan Kim: Private DNS is a big one. In our environment, we have custom DNS resolvers and we forward queries. Sometimes private DNS on endpoints conflicts with our split-horizon.

[05:22] Victor Alvarez: Yeah. The module allows private DNS toggle for interface endpoints. Default is “on” because it’s simplest. But if you have centralized Route53 resolver rules, you might want it off and handle the records yourself.

[05:39] Priya Nair: If private DNS is off, does your installer still work?

[05:43] Colin O'Donnell: It can, but then you need to ensure the standard AWS service names resolve to the endpoint IPs in that VPC. So basically you take on responsibility for DNS mapping. Installer checks resolution; it doesn’t care how you achieved it.

[05:58] Anita Desai: Okay. That’s doable.

[06:02] Markus Klein: Jordan, can you share what region(s) you plan to run in? Some endpoints vary by partition, but standard commercial regions are pretty consistent.

[06:10] Jordan Kim: Initially us-east-1, maybe us-west-2 later.

[06:14] Victor Alvarez: Great. Our integration tests run a matrix across a couple regions, including those.

[06:19] Priya Nair: Logging: you said CloudWatch Logs endpoint. But we route logs to Splunk via Firehose, and flow logs we usually put into S3 for retention.

[06:31] Victor Alvarez: Totally. For VPC flow logs, our module supports either CloudWatch Logs or S3 as the destination. Default recommendation in the README is CloudWatch for faster troubleshooting, but S3 is very common for retention/compliance.

[06:48] Victor Alvarez: For Redwood component logs, the platform can ship to CloudWatch and then you can export, or we can configure log forwarding to your collector depending on your setup. In alpha, the simplest supported path is CloudWatch Logs.

[07:04] Priya Nair: Is flow logs “on” by default in your Terraform?

[07:07] Victor Alvarez: In the reference module, flow logs are enabled by default with a sane retention if using CloudWatch, but you can turn it off. Security typically wants it on; some customers choose to manage flow logs centrally.

[07:21] Anita Desai: Our preference is: we enable it but route to our central S3 bucket with KMS. Can your module support a bucket we pass in?

[07:29] Victor Alvarez: Yes, you can pass existing bucket ARN and KMS key ARN. If you don’t pass, it can create resources, but for enterprise we usually “bring your own”.

[07:41] Jordan Kim: On the VPC topology: Do you require public subnets?

[07:45] Victor Alvarez: Not strictly. Public subnets only matter if you’re creating NAT gateways in that VPC. If you do no NAT and no IGW, you can skip public tier entirely. Our wrapper module has toggles; it won’t create IGW if you’re in private-only mode.

[08:03] Jordan Kim: And your “isolated” subnets, are those where you place the control plane components?

[08:08] Colin O'Donnell: For Redwood Private: the “control plane” is deployed in your VPC but managed by our installer. We typically put the most sensitive internal services in isolated, but it depends on what needs to talk out. If everything they need is reachable via endpoints, isolated is fine.

[08:27] Markus Klein: The key is: ECR pulls, S3 access, logs. If those are via endpoints and DNS works, you can keep it fully private.

[08:35] Priya Nair: What about time sync, NTP? Some appliances choke on that.

[08:39] Victor Alvarez: Good question. Usually AWS managed NTP is reachable inside VPC without internet. If you use custom NTP, that’s on your side. We don’t require outbound NTP to the public internet.

[08:52] Anita Desai: Okay.

[08:54] Colin O'Donnell: Let me ask: do you want to deploy into an existing VPC, or create a new one dedicated to Redwood.

[09:00] Anita Desai: Existing, ideally. New VPC is possible but politically hard. We can carve new subnets though.

[09:08] Victor Alvarez: Then you’ll like the “existing VPC adoption mode”. It basically consumes existing VPC ID and subnet IDs. We still set up endpoints and security groups and flow logs if you want. We purposely disable combinations that are unsafe like “existing VPC but also create overlapping subnets”.

[09:28] Jordan Kim: Can you create endpoints into subnets we choose? For example we want interface endpoints only in the private subnets, not isolated.

[09:35] Victor Alvarez: Yes, you pass a list of subnet IDs for endpoint ENIs. Default is private tier.

[09:45] Priya Nair: Security groups baseline — what’s included? We will not allow wide egress.

[09:51] Victor Alvarez: Baseline SGs are least-privilege by default. We scope ingress to internal traffic between components. For egress, we generally recommend restricting to VPC endpoints prefix lists / security groups rather than 0.0.0.0/0.

[10:10] Victor Alvarez: That said, some AWS services don’t map cleanly to prefix lists for interface endpoints, so we often do “egress to endpoint SG” pattern: allow egress only to the security group attached to the endpoint ENIs.

[10:25] Jordan Kim: Yup, we do that.

[10:27] Priya Nair: Are NACLs part of the module?

[10:30] Victor Alvarez: We intentionally didn’t over-opinionate NACLs in alpha because it can conflict with existing enterprise standards. We document guidance, but we mostly handle security via SGs. Some customers have centralized NACL policies.

[10:47] Anita Desai: That’s fine.

[10:49] Markus Klein: Priya, any compliance requirement around tagging? Like cost center, data class.

[10:55] Priya Nair: Yes, we require owner, environment, and data classification tags. And our security tooling checks them.

[11:03] Victor Alvarez: Our modules follow a standard tagging schema: cost-center, env, owner, data-class. You can pass a map and we propagate to all resources.

[11:18] Colin O'Donnell: Maybe we go a level deeper on endpoints. Jordan, do you do private-only Docker pulls today from ECR without NAT?

[11:26] Jordan Kim: Yes, for some clusters. We use ECR api and dkr endpoints plus S3 gateway, and private DNS enabled. But we also had to add something else once—maybe STS, like you said.

[11:41] Colin O'Donnell: Yeah, that sounds right.

[11:43] Priya Nair: Wait, why does S3 matter for ECR again? We thought ECR endpoints cover it.

[11:49] Victor Alvarez: ECR uses S3 under the hood for image layers. Even if you can hit ECR, downloads can fail without S3 access. That’s why we always include S3 gateway endpoint in the baseline.

[12:05] Priya Nair: Got it.

[12:06] Anita Desai: Does Redwood pull images from your ECR or ours?

[12:10] Colin O'Donnell: For Private, we deliver images to your environment; depending on the deployment mode it may be your ECR or our distribution mechanism, but from your VPC perspective the requirement is: whatever registry endpoints we use must be reachable. In most AWS-native installs, it’s ECR endpoints.

[12:30] Markus Klein: And we’ll validate that with you in the pilot checklist.

[12:33] Jordan Kim: If we route everything through TGW to our proxy, can we skip endpoints?

[12:39] Victor Alvarez: You can, but we strongly recommend endpoints for reliability and to avoid surprises. Proxy adds another moving piece, and some orgs block certain AWS domains. Also endpoints keep traffic on the AWS backbone.

[12:54] Priya Nair: From security, endpoints are preferred.

[12:56] Anita Desai: Same.

[12:58] Colin O'Donnell: Great. So “private-only endpoints, no IGW, no NAT” is a supported pattern in our examples.

[13:06] Markus Klein: We have a locked-down example configuration that literally does that. It’s basically: private subnets + isolated subnets, endpoints enabled, and no public egress.

[13:18] Anita Desai: Nice. That’s the one we want.

[13:20] Colin O'Donnell: Cool, we’ll send the quickstart and that example tfvars.

[13:24] Jordan Kim: Question on Route53: if endpoints have private DNS enabled, it hijacks the public AWS names, right?

[13:31] Victor Alvarez: Yep. For example, ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com will resolve to the endpoint inside the VPC. That’s the intended behavior. But if you have custom resolver rules, you might have to coordinate.

[13:49] Jordan Kim: Our resolver rules sometimes forward *.amazonaws.com to a central resolver. That could conflict.

[13:55] Victor Alvarez: Exactly. In that case, two options:
1) Keep private DNS enabled, but ensure the VPC uses the AmazonProvidedDNS and not overridden resolvers, or
2) Disable private DNS on endpoints and create explicit private hosted zone records or conditional forwarding rules.

[14:14] Priya Nair: Is there a preflight that checks DNS specifically? Like not just reachability.

[14:19] Colin O'Donnell: Yes, it checks that name resolves and that the resolved IP is reachable. It’ll also print what it resolved to, so you can see if it’s going to public internet versus the VPC endpoint.

[14:33] Anita Desai: That’s helpful.

[14:35] Markus Klein: Also, we have troubleshooting docs that cover “ECR pulls failing” and it’s usually DNS or missing endpoint. Like 80%.

[14:46] Jordan Kim: (laughs) yeah, that’s our life too.

[14:48] Colin O'Donnell: Same.

[14:50] Priya Nair: On encryption hooks: If flow logs go to S3, can we enforce KMS?

[14:56] Victor Alvarez: Yes, you can specify the KMS key for the bucket and we recommend bucket policies that require SSE-KMS. The module won’t magically override your org policy, but it supports the inputs.

[15:10] Anita Desai: Great.

[15:12] Colin O'Donnell: Time-to-deploy wise: what we’ve seen is customers spending two to four weeks getting the network “just right” when it’s bespoke. The alpha modules aim to make it like a couple hours to apply and then run installer.

[15:28] Jordan Kim: That’s attractive. We’re trying to hit a March pilot.

[15:32] Markus Klein: That’s doable. The big gating is DNS and endpoint approvals.

[15:38] Priya Nair: And security review.

[15:40] Colin O'Donnell: Right.

[15:42] Victor Alvarez: One more nuance: endpoint policies. In alpha we include policy stubs and let you tighten them. Some orgs lock S3 endpoint policies down to specific buckets. For ECR, policies can get tricky.

[16:00] Jordan Kim: We do restrict S3 endpoint to specific buckets. For ECR we usually don’t because it breaks too easily.

[16:07] Victor Alvarez: That’s consistent with our guidance. Start permissive for functionality, then tighten.

[16:15] Priya Nair: Could you provide a minimal set of AWS IAM permissions needed to apply the Terraform? Our infra team is strict.

[16:22] Markus Klein: Yes, the quickstart includes required IAM, and we can also send a policy doc. But roughly it’s ec2:CreateVpc, CreateSubnet, CreateVpcEndpoint, logs permissions, iam role for flow logs, etc.

[16:40] Colin O'Donnell: In existing VPC mode, it’s less because you’re not creating VPC/subnets.

[16:45] Anita Desai: That’s important for us. We likely can’t let a module create VPCs.

[16:50] Victor Alvarez: Then you’ll use that mode.

[16:53] Jordan Kim: What about IPv6? We’re starting to roll it out.

[16:56] Victor Alvarez: Alpha focuses on IPv4. IPv6 is on the roadmap, but not something we claim as supported in the reference modules yet.

[17:05] Jordan Kim: Okay.

[17:07] Priya Nair: You mentioned “control plane” earlier. Any inbound requirements? Like do we need to allow inbound from Redwood cloud.

[17:14] Colin O'Donnell: For Private VPC deployments, everything stays within your VPC. We don’t require inbound from Redwood’s hosted environment. There can be optional integrations (updates, telemetry) but those can be disabled or routed through your approved paths.

[17:30] Priya Nair: Good.

[17:31] Markus Klein: The installer may need to pull artifacts; that’s where endpoints come in.

[17:36] Jordan Kim: If we do no egress, how do updates work.

[17:41] Colin O'Donnell: In fully locked-down mode, updates are more controlled. We can do an approved artifact import process. For alpha pilot we typically use AWS-native artifact pulls via endpoints, and version pinning.

[17:56] Anita Desai: Okay.

[17:58] Victor Alvarez: One more callout: CloudWatch Logs endpoint. Some customers say “we don’t use CloudWatch”. But if we can’t reach CloudWatch and you don’t have alternate log pipeline configured, troubleshooting gets hard. So we at least recommend enabling the endpoint even if you export to Splunk.

[18:17] Priya Nair: That’s fine. We can enable it.

[18:20] Jordan Kim: We also use GuardDuty and AWS Config. Not relevant probably.

[18:23] Victor Alvarez: Not directly. But tags and flow logs help.

[18:28] Colin O'Donnell: We’ve got about 25 minutes left. Anything else in your architecture we should account for? TGW, shared DNS, etc.

[18:38] Jordan Kim: The big one is: our private hosted zones are in a central account. Workload accounts associate to them via RAM. We can associate another PHZ if needed but it requires a ticket.

[18:51] Victor Alvarez: In most cases you don’t need your own PHZ if you use endpoint private DNS. But if you disable endpoint private DNS and do custom records, then yes you’ll need PHZ.

[19:06] Jordan Kim: Got it.

[19:08] Anita Desai: What about Route53 Resolver inbound/outbound endpoints? We have them already.

[19:13] Victor Alvarez: That’s fine. Just ensure the VPC where Redwood runs can resolve AWS service domains to the endpoint IPs. If your resolver forwards amazonaws.com elsewhere, we should test.

[19:27] Colin O'Donnell: We can do a short preflight test without deploying everything. Like create endpoints, then run the installer preflight. That will surface DNS issues early.

[19:38] Priya Nair: That would be ideal.

[19:40] Markus Klein: Agreed.

[19:42] Anita Desai: We also have requirement that subnets are /24 and not bigger. Any issue?

[19:48] Victor Alvarez: Not really, as long as you have enough IPs for endpoint ENIs and the components. Interface endpoints consume ENIs per subnet; it adds up. We can help size it. /24 per subnet is usually okay but if you do a lot of endpoints across three AZs you can run tight.

[20:10] Jordan Kim: Yeah, we’ve hit IP exhaustion before.

[20:12] Victor Alvarez: Exactly. That’s why we typically recommend at least /23 or /22 for endpoint-heavy VPCs. But if you’re stuck with /24, we can limit endpoints to fewer subnets and rely on cross-AZ routing, though that’s not ideal.

[20:30] Anita Desai: Hmm. We might be able to do /23.

[20:33] Colin O'Donnell: If you share your CIDR plan we can sanity check.

[20:38] Priya Nair: On the security group rules: do you have a list of ports required between components.

[20:44] Victor Alvarez: Yes, baseline SG module includes typical ports; and variables let you override if you have custom ports. We validate they’re within ranges.

[20:58] Markus Klein: We’ll also provide the “networking requirements” doc listing ports and endpoint requirements.

[21:05] Anita Desai: Great.

[21:06] Jordan Kim: Are you using Kubernetes? Because our EKS clusters are in private subnets.

[21:12] Colin O'Donnell: Redwood Private can be deployed into Kubernetes in your environment. The network requirements remain: the nodes/pods need to reach endpoints for pulls and logs. If you already run EKS private, this should feel familiar.

[21:29] Jordan Kim: Okay.

[21:30] Priya Nair: How does this compare to, say, just running vLLM in our cluster.

[21:35] Markus Klein: Totally fair. With self-hosted vLLM you own the whole ops surface: upgrades, perf tuning, observability, fallbacks. Redwood gives you a production platform and a consistent control plane, plus the secure-by-default deployment patterns. This Terraform effort is about making the private deployment less painful.

[21:58] Priya Nair: Okay.

[22:00] Colin O'Donnell: Let’s do a quick recap of “required” for your desired mode:
- Existing VPC + new subnets as needed
- VPC endpoints: ECR api, ECR dkr, S3 gateway, CloudWatch Logs, STS
- Private DNS: either enabled on endpoints OR you handle records
- No IGW / no NAT, unless you choose centralized egress
- Flow logs to S3 with your KMS

[22:30] Jordan Kim: Yes.

[22:31] Anita Desai: Yep.

[22:32] Priya Nair: And security groups restricted to endpoints, not open egress.

[22:36] Victor Alvarez: Exactly.

[22:38] Colin O'Donnell: Perfect.

[22:40] Markus Klein: Next steps from Redwood side: we’ll send the quickstart, plus the locked-down example and endpoint list. Then schedule a follow-up where you share the TGW diagram and DNS resolver behavior.

[22:54] Anita Desai: Works.

[22:56] Jordan Kim: Can you include the part about IP sizing? That’s helpful for our subnet request.

[23:00] Victor Alvarez: Yep, I’ll add a note.

[23:03] Priya Nair: And please include what logs go where, at least at a high level.

[23:07] Colin O'Donnell: Will do.

[23:10] (crosstalk)

[23:12] Markus Klein: Sorry, Priya, say again?

[23:14] Priya Nair: Just a high level: what you log, and where it lands by default.

[23:18] Colin O'Donnell: Yep, we’ll include that. By default: application/service logs to CloudWatch Logs if enabled, and VPC flow logs to S3 or CloudWatch depending on config.

[23:29] Priya Nair: Great.

[23:31] Colin O'Donnell: Any last questions before we wrap?

[23:35] Anita Desai: Not from me.

[23:36] Jordan Kim: All good.

[23:37] Priya Nair: Good.

[23:39] Colin O'Donnell: Alright. We’ll send materials by tomorrow and propose times for next week. Thanks everyone.

[23:46] Meeting ended.
